topic.en: Three texts: how the container rebuilt world trade, how migrating birds navigate, and what is known about homework.
topic.kk: Үш мәтін: контейнер әлемдік сауданы қалай өзгертті, жыл құстары немен бағдарлайды және үй тапсырмасының пайдасы туралы не белгілі.
topic.ru: Три текста: как контейнер перестроил мировую торговлю, по чему ориентируются перелётные птицы и что известно о пользе домашних заданий.

paragraphs.text: Before the container, loading a ship was a craft. Sacks, barrels, crates and bales arrived at the quay in whatever shape their owners had chosen, and gangs of dockers stowed them by hand, fitting awkward objects together like a puzzle that had to be solved again for every voyage. A ship could spend as long in port as at sea. Loading costs made up a large share of the price of moving anything, and theft along the way was so ordinary that it was written into insurance rates. The trade that resulted was mostly regional: it made sense to buy from the next country, not from the far side of the world.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The idea that ended this was not a technology but a shape. A steel box of agreed dimensions can be filled by the shipper, sealed, lifted by crane, set on a lorry or a railway wagon and opened only at its destination. Nothing inside is handled in between. The first container voyage, from one American port to another in 1956, carried fifty-eight boxes on a converted tanker, and the saving was immediate: the cost of loading a tonne of cargo fell by something close to ninety-five per cent. The invention itself was simple enough that nobody could patent the concept, which is one reason it spread.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Spreading, however, took twenty years, because a box is only useful if everyone agrees on it. Early operators built containers to their own sizes, and a box that would not fit a competitor’s crane or a foreign railway wagon was a liability rather than an asset. Agreement came through a long and unglamorous standards process, which fixed the corner fittings, the lengths and the stacking strength that the whole system now relies on. The corner fitting matters more than it sounds: it is the reason a box made anywhere can be locked to a ship made anywhere, by a crane operator who has never seen either before.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The consequences ran far beyond shipping. Because moving goods became cheap and predictable, a factory no longer had to sit near its customers or its suppliers, and production could be broken into pieces and sent wherever each piece was cheapest to make. The parts of a single machine might cross three oceans before it is sold. Ports moved too. The old docks lay in the middle of cities, surrounded by warehouses and by the districts where dockers lived; container terminals need deep water, flat land and motorway access, so the business left for estuaries and reclaimed ground, and the city centres it left behind were rebuilt as offices and flats.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The people who had made the old system work did not survive it. Dock labour fell by four fifths in most large ports within a generation, and the work that remained needed different skills: a modern terminal is run by a handful of crane operators and a planning office, and much of the yard is moved by machines that follow instructions from software. In several countries the change was fought bitterly and settled with agreements that paid older dockers to leave. The disappearance was not gradual; in some ports the whole trade went within a decade of the first container crane.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The system has its own weaknesses, and they are the weaknesses of anything standardised. A sealed box is hard to inspect, which suits smugglers as well as exporters; customs services now work largely from paperwork, risk scoring and scanners rather than from opening doors. Because the boxes are interchangeable, they pile up wherever trade is unbalanced, and empty containers are shipped back across the world at a loss. And a network built for efficiency has little slack: when one link jams, as happened when a single ship blocked a canal, the queue forms everywhere at once.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: It is tempting to call the container the cause of modern trade, and economists have tried to measure it. The honest finding is that it was necessary rather than sufficient: cheap boxes mattered because tariffs were falling, ships were getting larger and communications were getting better at the same time. What can be said is narrower and still remarkable. A shape agreed by committee, which no one owns and which contains nothing of interest in itself, rearranged where the world makes things and who is paid for handling them.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Every autumn a small bird weighing less than a bar of soap leaves northern Europe, crosses the Sahara and arrives in a patch of West African woodland it has used before. It travels alone, often at night, and in many species the young birds make the first journey without an adult to follow. Whatever guides them is carried in the bird, not learned from company. The question of what that is has occupied biologists for a century, and the answer has turned out to be several things at once. No single sense would survive the journey on its own, and the interesting part is how the senses are combined.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first clue came from a cage. In the 1950s a German researcher noticed that migratory birds kept indoors became restless at exactly the season they would have left, and hopped repeatedly towards one side of the cage — the side facing the direction of migration. Recording that restlessness turned migration into something that could be studied in a laboratory: change what the bird can see, or the magnetic field around the cage, and see which way it hops. Almost everything known about avian navigation has been built on that simple observation.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Birds read the sky. Species that migrate by day use the sun, correcting for its movement with an internal clock, so that the same angle means a different direction at breakfast and at dusk. Night migrants use the stars, but not as sailors do: hand-raised birds shown an artificial sky learn the pattern of rotation around the celestial pole, and take that still point, rather than any particular constellation, as north. A bird raised under a planetarium sky that rotated around the wrong star grew up with a correspondingly wrong idea of north.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: They also read the earth. Birds sense the magnetic field, and they use it in two ways: as a compass, which tells direction, and as a rough map, because the angle at which the field meets the ground changes predictably from the equator to the poles. The compass appears to sit in the eye. A class of light-sensitive proteins in the retina reacts differently depending on the field, which would make direction something the bird sees rather than feels, and the mechanism fails under certain wavelengths of light — a bird in red light loses its bearings, though it can see perfectly well.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Smell has proved the most controversial sense on the list. Experiments with homing pigeons whose sense of smell was blocked showed birds that circled uncertainly and took far longer to return, which suggested a map built from airborne scents carried on prevailing winds. The result has been reproduced many times in some species and not at all in others, and the argument about what it means has run for four decades. What is agreed is narrower: some birds use some odours over some distances, and no one claims smell alone could cross a desert. The disagreement is a good example of how a field argues: not about whether the birds arrive, but about which of several explanations the data actually support.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Modern tracking has replaced ringing, and the picture it gives is untidier than the textbooks. Tags weighing under a gram record light levels, from which a rough position can be reconstructed, and larger birds carry satellite transmitters that report continuously. The data show individuals taking different routes in different years, stopping for weeks at places nobody knew were important, and correcting course after storms in ways a simple compass could not explain. Navigation, it seems, is less a single instrument than a set of overlapping ones, checked against each other and against memory of the ground below. A bird that loses one of them usually still arrives; a bird that loses several does not.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: This matters beyond the science, because the journeys are getting harder. Light at night draws night migrants off course and holds them circling over cities; glass towers kill them in numbers that are only now being counted; and the stopover sites where a bird doubles its weight before crossing a desert are exactly the wetlands that are easiest to drain. Protecting a migratory species means protecting a chain of places thousands of kilometres apart, any one of which can break the journey. Understanding how the birds navigate is the easy part; keeping the route usable is not.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Few school practices are defended as confidently and studied as inconclusively as homework. Parents assume it raises results, teachers assume it is expected of them, and ministries publish guidance on how many minutes a child of each age should be given. The research, when it is gathered, supports a much narrower claim than any of them would like, and it says different things at different ages. The argument that follows is therefore not about whether children should work at home, but about what the work is for. Four people who have spent their careers inside that question disagree about almost everything except one thing: the usual defence of homework is weaker than it sounds, and the usual attack on it is broader than the evidence allows.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Elena Marchetti has spent two decades pooling the measurements. The pattern she reports is consistent and awkward: in the last years of school, time spent on homework correlates with better results, and the correlation is respectable; in primary school it is close to zero, and in the middle years it sits somewhere between. Correlation is doing a lot of work in those sentences, she adds, because the households that produce hours of completed homework differ in many other ways. What can be said with more confidence is that beyond about two hours a night the relationship flattens and then turns down.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Joseph Oduya argues that the measurements miss the point by counting minutes. A worksheet that repeats what the class has already understood teaches nothing and takes an hour; ten minutes of retrieval practice, spaced a few days after the lesson, moves material into long-term memory and is supported by evidence that has nothing to do with homework research. The variable that matters is not how long a child works at home but what kind of task it is, and almost no study records that. Until it does, he says, the field is measuring the wrong thing carefully. His own proposal is dull and cheap: record the task, not the clock, and half the contradictions in the literature would resolve themselves within a few years.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Fatima Zaidi looks at who is in the room. Homework is schoolwork done in conditions the school does not control: a desk or a shared kitchen table, a quiet flat or a noisy one, a parent who can explain quadratic equations or a parent working a night shift. Set the same task to a whole class and it will be completed in wildly different circumstances, so the gap between children widens rather than narrows. Her conclusion is not to abolish it but to change where it happens: supervised study time inside the school day, she argues, delivers the practice without exporting it to unequal homes. She notes that this costs staff time, which is the real reason it is rare, and that the schools which have tried it report the loudest objections from parents rather than from children.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Bjorn Halvorsen points out that the countries usually held up as models disagree with each other. One much-admired system sets very little homework and performs well; another sets a great deal and also performs well. Comparisons of this kind, he warns, are nearly useless on their own, because the systems differ in teacher training, class size, curriculum and how much private tutoring goes on outside school, and tutoring in particular is invisible in the official figures. A country that appears to set no homework may simply have moved it to a paid classroom in the evening. Until surveys count that hour as work, he argues, league tables of homework describe what schools set rather than what children actually do.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Where does that leave a teacher on Monday? With less licence than the tradition assumes and more than its critics allow. The defensible version is short, spaced, aimed at remembering rather than finishing, marked in a way that tells the child something, and set in the knowledge that some children have nowhere quiet to do it. The indefensible version is a worksheet assigned because the timetable says Monday, and the honest thing to say about the evidence is that it has never supported the indefensible version at all. A teacher who applies that single filter will set less work, mark it better, and be able to explain to any parent why the pile of paper got smaller. That is a smaller promise than the tradition makes and a larger one than the evidence has ever been asked to keep.
paragraphs.label: F
